title: Why Did Outlook Go Down Worldwide?

retention_map.cause: front door, July fix, sleeper bug, pile-on, domino effect
retention_map.conclusion: mail not lost; check; backup; final joke; standard end card (automatic)

scenes.title: Outlook Stops
scenes.retention_hook: Instant hook: the Outlook spinner that never stops

dialogue.text: On Thursday, November twelfth, millions of people suddenly could not open Outlook.
Where are my emails?!
It is just spinning!

actions: Guy at a desk stares at a laptop with a never-ending spinner
Banker storms in demanding his emails
Envelopes pile up outside the laptop

scenes.title: The Spike
scenes.retention_hook: First surprise: 129,000 error reports in about half an hour

dialogue.text: Around midday Eastern, error reports spiked. Within about half an hour, more than one hundred twenty nine thousand problem reports had been logged on Downdetector, a site that tracks outages.
My phone will not stop ringing!

actions: Error-report graph spikes
Counter climbs to 129,000+
IT Friend's phone rings nonstop

scenes.title: What Else Broke
scenes.retention_hook: Escalation: it was not only Outlook; Exchange Online is the shared engine

dialogue.text: It was not only Outlook. Anything relying on Exchange Online, Microsoft's email engine, struggled: Teams calendars, Copilot, and parts of SharePoint. Teams chat and calls mostly kept working. Microsoft reports over four hundred fifty million paid business seats.

actions: Hub diagram: Exchange Online in the middle
Red crosses on Outlook, Teams calendar, Copilot, SharePoint features
Green check on Teams chat and calls
Counter: 450 million+ business seats

scenes.title: Not a Hack
scenes.retention_hook: New mystery: if it was not an attack, what was it?

dialogue.text: So, was it a hack? Microsoft said no. It called it a technical issue, not related to cyber attacks or AI.
Phew!
Then what broke?

actions: NOT A CYBERATTACK stamp slams
Guy sighs with relief; Friend asks what broke
scenes.note: Source: Microsoft statement via ABC News

scenes.title: The Front Door
scenes.retention_hook: Big reveal part 1: all mail traffic goes through front-door servers; a July fix

dialogue.text: Here is what Microsoft's preliminary report says. Mail traffic passes through special front-door servers. In July, Microsoft rolled out a Windows fix just for those servers, and it ran smoothly for more than three months.

actions: Envelopes stream through a big front door
A July calendar page gets a checkmark
A timer counts up past 3 months of no problems
scenes.note: Source: Microsoft preliminary report via Office Watch

scenes.title: The Sleeper Bug
scenes.retention_hook: Big reveal part 2: a sleeper bug the lab never found

dialogue.text: But the fix hid a sleeper bug. Under heavy load on newer, more powerful servers, the machines could lock up. Microsoft's lab tests used weaker hardware, so they never caught it.
But it worked in the lab!

actions: A bug sleeps under a rug
Small lab machine: everything fine
Big new server under load: lock up
scenes.note: Source: Microsoft preliminary report via Office Watch

scenes.title: Piling On
scenes.retention_hook: Escalation: two more things piled on that day

dialogue.text: On the day, two more things piled on. About fifteen hours earlier, Teams traffic had been moved onto the same front door. And nearly fourteen percent of the server capacity was already out of service from an unrelated problem.

actions: Teams crowd shoves into the front door
One server in seven goes dark: 14% out
scenes.note: Source: Microsoft preliminary report via Office Watch

scenes.title: The Domino Effect
scenes.retention_hook: New mystery resolved: servers lock up one after another

dialogue.text: At the busiest time of the US business day, servers locked up. The safety net moved traffic to healthy servers, which then locked up too. In under two hours, more than eighty percent had stopped responding.
Is that normal?

actions: Row of servers falls one by one like dominoes
Counter climbs to 80%+
scenes.note: Source: Microsoft preliminary report via Office Watch

scenes.title: The Slow Recovery
scenes.retention_hook: Escalation: why fixing it took so long, then the rollback in batches

dialogue.text: Recovery was slow. Restarted servers were swamped by waiting traffic, and the usual undo did not help, because the change was months old. Engineers rolled back the code and restored servers in batches, Asia Pacific first, then Europe.
Have you tried turning it off and on again?

actions: Restarted servers get swamped
Undo button does nothing
Code rolled back; servers return in batches: Asia Pacific, then Europe
scenes.note: Source: Microsoft preliminary report via Office Watch

scenes.title: Back to Normal

dialogue.text: By Friday morning, Eastern time, webmail was back to normal worldwide. Microsoft marked the incident fully restored late Friday, after the backlog of email had been processed.

actions: Timeline from Thursday midday to Friday night
Friday morning: webmail normal worldwide
Late Friday: fully restored, backlog processed
scenes.note: Sources: Microsoft, Office Watch, ABC News

scenes.title: Conclusion: Check Your Mail
scenes.retention_hook: Conclusion + final joke: delayed mail was not lost; check; keep a backup

dialogue.text: The good news: delayed email was not lost, because Microsoft gave messages extra time to be delivered. Still, if you sent something important on Thursday or Friday, check that it arrived, and keep a backup way to reach people.
I will print all my emails!
Please, not again!

actions: Checklist ticks: mail not lost; check what you sent; have a backup
Banker threatens to print his emails; Guy begs him not to
scenes.note: Source: Microsoft preliminary report via Office Watch
